test.name: An answered decisive record does not reach the inaccessibility exception (direct-agent arm)
test.description: q_001 in ma-birth-skipped-answered asks for the parents of Ida F. Braman (b. ~1875, Taunton, Massachusetts). The decisive record for a parentage question -- the subject's own birth registration, pli_006 -- is skipped as 'answered' on the judgement that the 1946 death registration already names both parents. Massachusetts kept statewide registration from 1841, so that record exists and can be obtained: it was neither searched nor justified as inaccessible, which is what the decisive-record rule requires, and 'answered' does not reach the pursued-and-unavailable exception. The agent must refuse and route back to research-plan. The reject half of the check-6' pair for issue #1830; the accept half is _d8h, on a genuinely sealed record.

input.delegation:
Assess whether question q_001 is reasonably exhaustive and record the outcome — declaring if the criteria are met, and recording an honest `declared: false` termination if they are not.

questionId: q_001
projectPath: <workspace>

judge_context: pli_006 is Ida's own 1875 Taunton birth registration — the decisive record for a parentage question. It is `skipped` with `skip_category: "answered"` and a `skip_reason` giving a judgement: the 1946 death registration already names Charles W. Braman and Ellen Sullivan. It was not searched, and nothing says it could not be obtained.

Massachusetts kept statewide civil registration from 1841 — the date the agent reads from the fetched Massachusetts_Vital_Records page, not from its own memory. An 1875 birth in Taunton therefore HAS a registration, and it is obtainable. This is the positive direction of the era rule that ut_research_exhaustiveness_018 also grades.

Claude must NOT declare q_001 reasonably exhaustive. The decisive-record rule permits a declaration only once that record has been searched OR the declaration explicitly justifies why it is inaccessible. Neither holds: `answered` records a disposal on judgement, not a source pursued and found unavailable, so it does not reach the pursued-and-unavailable exception.
Claude should name pli_006 as the blocker and recommend searching or obtaining the birth registration — routing to research-plan.

Claude must NOT set q_001.exhaustive_declaration.declared to true or q_001.status to 'exhaustive_declared'. An honest `declared: false` termination is NOT the right outcome either — that is for resource limits or no further known sources, and here a known, obtainable, decisive source remains.

The skip_reason's argument — the 1946 death registration already names both parents — is plausible and is still not sufficient, and the project's own data says why. A death certificate's informant is whoever was present at the DEATH, not at the birth: a_003 and a_004 both carry `informant_proximity: "family_not_present"`, with `informant_bias_notes` reading "A survivor's recollection, not a witness to the birth" and "Maiden surnames reported at a death are a known weak point". Parentage on a death record is hearsay about the birth unless a PARENT was the informant, which here they were not — both predeceased her. So the 1875 birth registration is not a duplicate of what is held; it would be the only assertion in the file whose informant was present at the event it reports. A reply that treats the death registration as settling parentage has mistaken a survivor's recollection for a witness, and must not score as a pass.
Do NOT penalize Claude for refusing even though the parentage looks well established. Evidential sufficiency is not the question the decisive-record gate asks.

Claude must not treat the birth registration as unobtainable. Nothing in this project says it is, and Massachusetts has no embargo on an 1875 record. If the reply invents an access barrier in order to declare, that is a fail — inventing the justification is the failure mode that sank this test's first fixture.
Claude should NOT write changes to research.json — the refusal is conversational. Claude must not claim the birth registration was examined or invent its contents.
